traveler: Saint Thecla of Iconium (Thekla, Santa Tecla), protomartyr and equal to the apostles
title: The Window at Iconium: the fire, the beasts, and the rock that closed at Seleucia
years: c. 30-c. 120 (traditional life); text and cult, 2nd century onward
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Iconium, the house of Theocleia
stops.date_confidence: traditional, and unattested. No securely first-century source names Thecla; she appears in no canonical gospel, no undisputed Pauline letter, and not in canonical Acts. The birth year c. 30 is a back-calculation from the Acts of Paul and Thecla, itself composed in the later second century. The date orders the segment and attests nothing.
stops.campa: Iconium stands on the Lycaonian plain under the mountains, a Greek-speaking city of the Roman province, and in one of its better houses a widow named Theocleia raises a daughter. No account names a father. The girl is called Thecla, her mother's own name turned around, god and glory changing places. She is brought up toward the one future the house has planned: a good marriage into a good family, a dowry counted out, children, the property passing on intact. By the time she is seventeen the match with Thamyris, a man of the city, is settled.
suggested_refs: Ancient Iconium beneath the mound of Alaeddin Tepesi, modern Konya
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla, Alexander Walker trans., Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 8 (1886)
Wikipedia, 'Thecla' (fetched)
Wikipedia, 'Konya' (fetched)

stops.name: Iconium, Paul in the house of Onesiphorus
stops.date_confidence: traditional. A literary episode in a later-second-century text, not a documented event. The sons of Onesiphorus are a manuscript variant: Walker's Ante-Nicene Fathers translation reads Silas and Zeno, the Lipsius Greek and M. R. James read Simmias and Zeno. Not resolved here.
stops.campa: Onesiphorus goes out on the Lystra road with his wife Lectra and his two sons to meet a man he has never seen. He carries a description sent ahead by Titus and matches it against the travellers: small, bald, bowed in the legs, eyebrows meeting over a long nose, and at moments the face of an angel. He finds him, greets him, and brings him home. In the courtyard Paul begins to teach continence and the resurrection of the dead, and the neighbours come in to listen. The house shares a wall with Theocleia's.
stops.quote: a man small in size, bald-headed, bandy-legged, well-built, with eyebrows meeting, rather long-nosed, full of grace
stops.quote_source: Acts of Paul and Thecla 3, Walker trans., Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 8
suggested_refs: The physical description of Paul in Acts of Paul and Thecla 3, the earliest surviving portrait of him in any text
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla 3, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8, newadvent.org/fathers/0816.htm
Wikipedia, 'Acts of Paul and Thecla' (fetched)

stops.name: Iconium, three days and nights at the window
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Literary episode; no documented event underlies it.
stops.campa: Thecla does not leave the window for three days and three nights. She does not eat and she does not turn her head. She watches the women going in and out of the courtyard next door and listens to a voice she cannot see, telling her that a body kept whole becomes a temple and that there is a resurrection for those who keep it so. Theocleia calls up to her and gets no answer. Thamyris, the man she is promised to, is sent for and stands below the sill and calls her too. Her mother says she clings there like a spider on the wall.
stops.quote: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God: blessed are they that have kept the flesh chaste, for they shall become a temple of God: blessed are they that control themselves, for God shall speak with them.
stops.quote_source: Acts of Paul and Thecla 5-6, Walker trans., Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 8
suggested_refs: Byzantine icons of Thecla at the window, the standard iconographic type
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla 5-6, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8
Wikipedia, 'Acts of Paul and Thecla' (fetched), plot summary

stops.name: Iconium, Thamyris before the governor
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The governor is named Castelius in some manuscripts and Cestilius in others. No court record of any kind exists for this or any other proceeding in the narrative.
stops.campa: Thamyris gathers the elders of the city and takes his complaint to the governor, and the complaint is not about doctrine. It is about property. The stranger empties the marriage contracts of Iconium: young men lose their wives, and a bride-price already agreed evaporates into a promise of resurrection. The governor listens to the men who pay his city's taxes and has Paul bound and taken to the prison. Thecla is not charged, and her name is nowhere in the complaint.
stops.quote: he deprives young men of wives, and maidens of husbands, saying, There is for you a resurrection in no other way, unless you remain chaste
stops.quote_source: Acts of Paul and Thecla 12, Walker trans., Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 8
suggested_refs: The Roman law of betrothal and dowry in the provinces, the machinery the accusation actually turns on
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla 12, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8
Wikipedia, 'Acts of Paul and Thecla' (fetched)

stops.name: Iconium, the bracelets and the silver mirror
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Detail corrected in this pass: the bracelets go to the gatekeeper and the silver mirror to the jailor, per Walker, ANF vol. 8, ch. 18. Earlier summaries reverse the two.
stops.campa: That night Thecla takes the bracelets from her arms and gives them to the man at the gate, and gives a silver mirror to the jailor, and both doors open for her. She finds Paul in the dark and sits down at his feet and stays there, hearing the great things of God, until her household discovers the bed empty and comes looking. They find her in the cell, sitting on the ground at the prisoner's feet, bound to him in affection, and they take her out of it into the street.
stops.quote: Thecla by night having taken off her bracelets, gave them to the gatekeeper... she went in beside Paul, and, sitting at his feet, she heard the great things of God
stops.quote_source: Acts of Paul and Thecla 18, Walker trans., Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 8
suggested_refs: The prison of Iconium, unlocated; no structure survives or has been proposed
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla 18, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8, newadvent.org/fathers/0816.htm

stops.name: Iconium, the tribunal and her mother's demand
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Literary episode. The mother's petition for her daughter's burning is the narrative's own most-repeated detail and is present in every recension.
stops.campa: The governor puts the question plainly: why will she not marry Thamyris, as the law of the Iconians requires? Thecla stands and looks across at Paul and says nothing at all. It is her mother who breaks the silence, from the floor of the court, calling for fire, naming her daughter a wretch, and asking that the other women watching learn from what is done to her. Paul is flogged and driven out of the gate. The governor sentences Thecla to burn, granting her mother the petition her mother made.
stops.quote: Burn the wicked wretch; burn in the midst of the theatre her that will not marry
stops.quote_source: Acts of Paul and Thecla 20, Walker trans., Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 8
suggested_refs: Theocleia's petition, the single detail the later Greek endings never soften
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla 20, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8

stops.name: Iconium, the pyre in the theatre
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Literary episode; no court record exists. The pin follows the Iconium theatre pin already used in margarita_pelagia.journey.json for the same scene. Walker's text gives her age here as seventeen; modern devotional retellings say eighteen, back-calculating from the same text's seventy-two years in the cave and ninety years of life.
stops.campa: They bring her into the theatre, strip her, and stack the wood. The governor weeps. The crowd fills the tiers. Thecla makes the sign of the cross over the pile and climbs onto it herself, and the boys throw in the fire. The flame stands up around her and does not touch her. Then the ground rumbles under the theatre and a cloud comes over the top of it, heavy with water and hail, and empties itself into the bowl. The fire goes out. Some of the crowd are killed by the downpour. She walks out of the wet ash unburnt.
stops.quote: God, having compassion upon her, made an underground rumbling, and a cloud overshadowed them from above, full of water and hail; and all that was in the cavity of it was poured out
stops.quote_source: Acts of Paul and Thecla 22, Walker trans., Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 8
suggested_refs: The theatre of ancient Iconium, site of the extinguished pyre
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla 22, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8
Wikipedia, 'Acts of Paul and Thecla' (fetched): 'was miraculously saved by a storm'

stops.name: Outside Iconium, the tomb on the Daphne road
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The tomb is unnamed in the text and has never been located; the coordinates are an approximate placement just outside the ancient city and carry no site claim.
stops.campa: Paul is on the road to Daphne with Onesiphorus and the family, and for six days they lie in an open tomb beside the highway, fasting, praying that Thecla will not be burnt. Hunger settles it. A boy is sent back toward the city to buy bread and meets her walking out of it. She comes to the tomb and finds them at prayer among the burial shelves, and Onesiphorus's children spread their clothes out on the stone for her to sit on. The boy is still out on the road somewhere with the money for the bread.
suggested_refs: Roadside chamber tombs of the Lycaonian plain, the ordinary architecture the scene assumes
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla 23-24, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8

stops.name: Outside Iconium, the seal refused
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Literary episode, and the pivot of the entire later dispute: Paul's refusal here is what makes her self-baptism at Antioch a self-baptism rather than a delayed sacrament.
stops.campa: She tells Paul she will cut off her hair and follow him wherever he goes, and he answers that the times are shameless and she is beautiful, and that a worse trial than the fire may take her and she may not bear it. Give me only the seal in Christ, she says, and no temptation will touch me. He tells her to be patient and she will receive the water in its time. He does not baptize her at the tomb, and the next water she comes to is in an arena at Antioch, with the seals in it.
stops.quote: I shall cut my hair, and follow thee whithersoever thou mayst go. And he said: It is a shameless age, and thou art beautiful.
stops.quote_source: Acts of Paul and Thecla 25, Walker trans., Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 8
suggested_refs: Acts of Paul and Thecla 25, the refusal of the seal, read against the self-baptism at ch. 34
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla 25, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8

stops.name: Antioch of Pisidia, Alexander in the street
stops.date_confidence: traditional, and the geography is unstable. The text says only Antioch; tradition identifies it as Pisidian Antioch, whose coordinates are used here (Wikipedia, 'Pisidian Antioch', 38 deg 18' 22" N, 31 deg 11' 21" E, near Yalvac). margarita_pelagia.journey.json places the same episode at Antioch on the Orontes, 36.205 / 36.16, about 700 km away. The divergence is flagged in the report and not resolved.
stops.campa: In Antioch a man named Alexander, first among the citizens and rich enough to pay for the games, sees her walking beside Paul and asks to buy her from him. Paul says he does not know her and she is not his. Alexander takes that as permission and embraces her in the open street. Thecla will not endure it. She tears the cloak off his shoulders and pulls the crown from his head, and the first man of the city stands in the marketplace bare-headed with his cloak in her fist.
stops.quote: he, being of great power, himself embraced her in the street. But she would not endure it... And taking hold of Alexander, she tore his cloak, and pulled off his crown
stops.quote_source: Acts of Paul and Thecla 26, Walker trans., Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 8
suggested_refs: The excavated civic centre of Pisidian Antioch at Yalvac, Isparta province
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla 26, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8
Wikipedia, 'Pisidian Antioch' (fetched), for site and coordinates
Wikipedia, 'Acts of Paul and Thecla' (fetched), plot summary

stops.name: Antioch of Pisidia, condemned to the beasts
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Literary episode; no record of any such proceeding survives from either candidate Antioch.
stops.campa: Alexander does not accuse her of refusing him. He accuses her of sacrilege against his person and his office, and brings her before the governor for the torn cloak and the crown in the dust. The court hears a magistrate insulted; it does not hear a woman assaulted. She is condemned to the wild beasts, and the games are Alexander's own to stage. The women of Antioch cry out from the back of the court that the judgement is wicked. The city keeps her under guard until the animals are ready.
suggested_refs: The women of Antioch as a chorus of protest, a structural feature of the narrative from ch. 27 to ch. 39
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla 27, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8

stops.name: Antioch of Pisidia, the house of Tryphaena
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Tryphaena's identification with the historical Pontic client queen Antonia Tryphaena, a Julio-Claudian relative, is a contested scholarly conjecture and is not established; the existing atlas prose in margarita_pelagia.journey.json states the kinship to Caesar as settled, which this file does not.
stops.campa: A rich widow of the city, kinswoman of Caesar by some accounts, asks to keep the condemned girl in her own house until the games. Tryphaena has buried a daughter, Falconilla, and Falconilla has come to her in a dream and asked that the stranger be received in her place and pray for her. So Thecla waits out the days not in a cell but in a house in mourning, sleeping in a dead girl's room, praying for a dead girl she never met, while the beasts are fed in their pens on the far side of the town.
stops.quote: A second mourning for my Falconilla has come upon my house and there is no one to help; neither child, for she is dead, nor kinsman, for I am a widow
stops.quote_source: Acts of Paul and Thecla 29, Walker trans., Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 8
suggested_refs: The disputed identification of Tryphaena with Antonia Tryphaena of Pontus, unresolved in the scholarship
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla 27-29, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8
Wikipedia, 'Acts of Paul and Thecla' (fetched)

stops.name: Antioch of Pisidia, the lioness in the arena
stops.date_confidence: traditional. This is the earliest narrative stratum of the whole Thecla tradition and the scene most often carved and painted afterwards.
stops.campa: On the first day they parade her through the city on the back of a lioness, seated, to be shown to the crowd before she is killed. The lioness licks her feet and the multitude stares. When the beasts are loosed in the arena it is this same animal that runs at the bear coming for Thecla and kills it, then goes at Alexander's lion and dies underneath it, killed defending her. The women in the tiers are shouting. Thecla stands out in the middle of the sand with her hands open, praying.
stops.quote: The lioness, with Thecla sitting upon her, licked her feet; and all the multitude was astonished
stops.quote_source: Acts of Paul and Thecla 33, Walker trans., Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 8
suggested_refs: Thecla between the beasts, the commonest image of her in late antique lamps, stelae and ampullae
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla 28, 33, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8
Wikipedia, 'Acts of Paul and Thecla' (fetched)

stops.name: Antioch of Pisidia, the pool of the seals
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The formula is quoted here in the Ante-Nicene Fathers wording; other atlas files and most summaries give a looser paraphrase, 'I baptize myself on the last day', which the ANF text does not support.
stops.campa: There is a tank in the arena full of man-eating seals, kept for the end of the day. Thecla sees the water and understands what it is for. Before the keepers can push her she turns to it herself and says that in the name of Jesus Christ she is baptized on her last day, and throws herself in. The lightning comes down into the water. The seals float up dead all round her, and a cloud of fire stands over the tank, so that no beast can reach her and no one in the tiers can see that she is naked.
stops.quote: In the name of Jesus Christ I am baptized on my last day.
stops.quote_source: Acts of Paul and Thecla 34, Walker trans., Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 8
suggested_refs: The seal-pool self-baptism, cited from the second century onward in the argument over whether women may baptize
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla 34, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8, newadvent.org/fathers/0816.htm
Wikipedia, 'Acts of Paul and Thecla' (fetched)

stops.name: Antioch of Pisidia, the bulls and the fainting of Tryphaena
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Literary episode.
stops.campa: They try the bulls next. Red-hot irons are put under the animals to madden them, and Thecla is tied between them by the feet. The flame burns through the ropes instead and she stands loose in the sand, untouched again. Alexander begs the governor to let it end; he has run out of animals and the crowd has turned against him. At the edge of the arena Tryphaena falls down beside the barrier and does not move, and word goes along the benches that the kinswoman of Caesar is dead. The games stop there.
suggested_refs: Roman provincial munera and the legal exposure of an editor whose spectacle killed a senatorial relative
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla 35-36, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8

stops.name: Antioch of Pisidia, released before the city
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Literary episode; the acclamation and the formula of release are the narrative's own, with no documentary parallel.
stops.campa: The governor calls for his clothes and has her brought out of the arena and asks who she is, and what she is wearing, that not one of the beasts would touch her. She answers that she is a servant of the living God, that she has believed in the Son of God in whom he is well pleased, and that this is why no animal laid a tooth on her. He orders garments brought and put on her, and has the release read out in front of the city: Thecla, the God-fearing servant of God, set free.
stops.quote: I indeed am a servant of the living God... I have believed in the Son of God, in whom He is well pleased
stops.quote_source: Acts of Paul and Thecla 37, Walker trans., Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 8
suggested_refs: The formula of manumission and release read publicly in a provincial arena
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla 37-38, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8

stops.name: Antioch of Pisidia, eight days in a converted household
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Literary episode. The cut mantle is the detail later writers reach for when they need a precedent for a woman in men's clothes.
stops.campa: Tryphaena, who is not dead, takes her home. For eight days Thecla lives in that house teaching the word of God, and most of the household believes, the widow among them; Tryphaena tells her that the dead daughter now has a sister. She is given gold and clothing to carry to Paul and to the poor. Then Thecla takes her mantle, cuts and stitches it into the shape of a man's travelling cloak, gathers the young men and maidens of the house about her, and goes out on the road to Myra.
suggested_refs: Jean Gerson, De Mirabili Victoria (Lyon, 14 May 1429), and Jacques Gelu, De Puella Aurelianensi (Embrun, 1429), both citing Thecla by name as precedent for a woman in men's dress
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla 39-40, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8
Wikipedia, 'Acts of Paul and Thecla' (fetched): 'wearing a mantle... made a man's cloak'

segments.name: The Cloak, and the Word to Teach

stops.name: Myra, finding Paul again
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Coordinates corrected in this pass: earlier summaries gave 36.2472 / 29.9828, which is modern Demre town centre, about 1.4 km from the ancient site. These are the coordinates of Myra itself, per Wikipedia's infobox.
stops.campa: She finds him in Myra, teaching. He looks at the figure in the man's cloak and does not know her at once, and when he does he takes her aside, astonished, and asks whether another trial has come on her and whether she has taken a husband. She tells him she has received the washing, and where. Paul takes her by the hand and brings her into the house of Hermias, and hears the whole of it out of her own mouth: the street, the court, the lioness, the water with the seals in it.
suggested_refs: Ancient Myra in Lycia, near modern Demre
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla 40, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8
Wikipedia, 'Myra' (fetched), for coordinates
Wikipedia, 'Acts of Paul and Thecla' (fetched)

stops.name: Myra, the word to teach
stops.date_confidence: traditional, and contested from antiquity. The commission stands in the common Greek ending. By c. AD 198-203 Tertullian is writing against exactly this sentence, reporting that the presbyter of Asia who composed the text was convicted, confessed he did it from love of Paul, and was removed from office.
stops.campa: Paul had refused her the seal at the tomb outside Iconium and told her to be patient. Now he hears that she gave it to herself in a tank of beasts, in front of a city, with no priest and no water blessed by anyone. He does not undo it, he does not reprove her, and nobody in the text asks him to. He tells her to go and teach the word of God. She takes the gold from Tryphaena's house, leaves the cloth for the poor in his hands, and turns back east toward Iconium.
stops.quote: Go, and teach the word of God.
stops.quote_source: Acts of Paul and Thecla 41, Walker trans., Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 8
suggested_refs: Tertullian, De Baptismo 17, c. AD 198-203, the earliest external notice of the text and an argument against this sentence
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla 41, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8
Tertullian, De Baptismo 17, ANF trans., newadvent.org/fathers/0321.htm (fetched)
Wikipedia, 'Acts of Paul and Thecla' (fetched)

stops.name: Iconium, the floor where he taught
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Literary episode.
stops.campa: Iconium takes her back as a stranger. She goes first to the house of Onesiphorus, which is empty now, and lies down on the floor of the room where she first heard the preaching through the wall, and weeps there, and prays. The wall she first listened through is still standing. Thamyris is dead: the man whose marriage contract set the whole machinery moving, the accusation and the fire and the road to Antioch, died while she was away. Nobody in Iconium now holds a legal claim on her.
suggested_refs: The house of Onesiphorus at Iconium, unlocated
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla 42, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8

stops.name: Iconium, at her mother's door
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The text does not narrate an answer. Some later recensions supply a conversion; the earliest do not, and the file follows the earliest.
stops.campa: Then she goes to her mother. Theocleia, who stood on the floor of the court and called for the fire, is living in the same house, and Thecla walks in and asks her whether she can believe that the Lord lives in heaven, and tells her that the God who gave her back her own life can give Theocleia hers, if it is money she wants, and can give her back her child, if it is a child she wants. The text does not say what her mother answers. It does not say she refuses, either. Thecla leaves the city and turns south.
suggested_refs: The house of Theocleia, and the silence at the end of ch. 43
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla 43, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8

stops.name: Seleucia ad Calycadnum, coming down out of the hills
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The earliest and shortest ending of the text gives her Seleucian years in a single clause and nothing else; everything after it in this segment comes from expanded endings and from the fifth-century Life and Miracles.
stops.campa: Seleucia sits where the Calycadnus comes down out of the Isaurian mountains to the sea, a Hellenistic foundation with a harbour, a garrison, and a great many gods. Thecla comes into it out of the hill country with nothing. She is a woman travelling alone in a cloak cut to the shape of a man's, into a city where nobody knows her name. The oldest and shortest telling of her life spends one line on everything that follows: she enlightened many with the word of God, and then she slept a good sleep.
suggested_refs: Silifke, ancient Seleucia ad Calycadnum, and its rock-cut necropolis
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla 43, short ending, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8
Wikipedia, 'Silifke' (fetched)
NASSCAL e-Clavis, 'Acts of Paul and Thecla' (fetched), on the eight distinct Greek endings

stops.name: Seleucia, the cave on the ridge
stops.date_confidence: traditional, from the expanded ending Walker prints as an appendix. The text's own numbers do not close: seventeen at the fire plus seventy-two in the cave is eighty-nine, against the same text's ninety years of life.
stops.campa: She does not live in the town. She goes up the ridge south of the walls to a cave in the rock and lives in it, on herbs and water, and stays there seventy-two years. Women come up from Seleucia to hear her and stay; the cave becomes a house of virgins on a hillside above a pagan city. She is a teacher with no church and a healer who takes no fee, and the sick who cannot climb are carried up to her. Nothing in the account says who feeds them, or who owns the ground the cave is cut in.
stops.quote: she departed to Seleucia, and dwelt in a cave seventy-two years, living upon herbs and water.
stops.quote_source: Acts of Paul and Thecla, expanded ending appended to ch. 43, Walker trans., Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 8
suggested_refs: Methodius of Olympus, Symposium, Discourse VIII and the concluding Hymn of Thecla at XI.2, making her the foremost of ten learned virgins
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla, expanded ending, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8
Methodius of Olympus, Symposium XI.2, ANF vol. 6, newadvent.org/fathers/062311.htm (fetched)
Wikipedia, 'Aya Tekla Church' (fetched)

stops.name: Seleucia, the cures that take no fee
stops.date_confidence: traditional, from the expanded Seleucian ending and the fifth-century Life and Miracles tradition. The date is an ordering device inside a life whose length the sources themselves cannot agree on.
stops.campa: What she does on the mountain costs nothing, and that is the trouble. The physicians of Seleucia keep a trade, and the sick who climb to the cave come back cured and do not pay. The doctors reason among themselves that she is a virgin and that the great Artemis attends her, and that if her virginity is taken the power will go out of her and the trade will come back. She is old by now; the number of her years in the cave is given as seventy-two. So they hire young men, fill them with wine, and send them up the hill.
suggested_refs: The rivalry of shrine healing and paid medicine in late antique Isauria
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla, expanded ending, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8
Life and Miracles of Saint Thecla (anon., 5th c., formerly attributed to Basil of Seleucia)

stops.name: Seleucia, the rock that closed
stops.date_confidence: traditional, and one of four incompatible endings. This is an aetiology for an empty or inaccessible tomb, and it competes directly with the recensions that give her a natural death and a burial at Seleucia, with the Maaloula version in which the rock opens instead, and with the version that takes her to Rome.
stops.campa: They come for her and she runs. There is nowhere on that hillside to run to. She stops at the rock face and prays, and the rock opens. She goes into the stone alive and it closes behind her. The account does not say how many men there were, or whether any of them was ever punished. What they are left holding is a piece of her veil, torn off as the rock closed, and that is the whole of what Seleucia has for a relic: cloth, and a face of stone with no seam in it. There is no grave here.
suggested_refs: The cave church at Ayatekla, cut into the rock beneath the later basilica
sources: Life and Miracles of Saint Thecla (anon., 5th c.)
Acts of Paul and Thecla, expanded Seleucian ending, Walker trans., ANF vol. 8

stops.name: Seleucia, the endings that do not agree
stops.date_confidence: attested as a fact about the manuscripts, not as an event. The stop is dated to the conventional composition of the Acts of Paul and Thecla in the later second century, and sits at the Seleucian pin because that is where every one of the disputed endings has to land. Manuscript figures from NASSCAL e-Clavis.
stops.campa: The Greek manuscripts do not agree about any of this. Eight distinct endings survive. One has her simply falling asleep at Seleucia and being buried there. One has the rock. One sends her on to Rome to die near Paul. The version that gives her the cave also gives her numbers, and the numbers do not add: seventeen years old at the fire, seventy-two years in the cave, and ninety years of life in all, which is one year more than the count allows. No recension corrects it.
suggested_refs: Lipsius and Bonnet, Acta Apostolorum Apocrypha (Leipzig, 1891-1903), the standard Greek text, from manuscripts A to M, all 10th to 12th century
sources: NASSCAL e-Clavis, 'Acts of Paul and Thecla' (fetched): 45+ Greek manuscripts, eight alternate endings, 135+ Latin manuscripts, Syriac, Coptic, Armenian, Arabic, Slavonic, Ethiopic
Papyrus witnesses P.Schoyen MS 2634.1 (3rd c.), P.Antinoopolis 13 (4th c.), P.Oxyrhynchus I 6 (5th c.)

segments.name: The Cult, and the Hill Above Silifke

stops.name: Iconium, the raid turned back in 354
stops.date_confidence: later tradition, absent from the second-century Acts. Reported by Wikipedia's Konya article and not verifiable beyond that secondary mention in this pass.
stops.campa: Three hundred years after she walked out of it, Iconium claims her back. The Isaurians come down out of the mountains in 354, and the city that burned her in its own theatre is saved from the raid by Thecla, and says so afterwards. There is nothing about this in the second-century book. It is the first addition the tradition makes that puts her back inside the walls that condemned her. Iconium has a bishop by then, and within twenty years it is the metropolitan see of Lycaonia.
suggested_refs: Konya as metropolitan see of Lycaonia from about 370, under Amphilochius as first metropolitan bishop
sources: Wikipedia, 'Konya' (fetched): 'saved the city from attack by the Isaurians in 354'

stops.name: Hagia Thekla, the cave under a church
stops.date_confidence: attested. A pilgrimage site existed here by 374; by 384 the shrine had monastic cells for men and for women, a central church, and an enclosing wall. The site lies about 1.5 to 2 km south of Silifke, which agrees with the pilgrim Egeria's 'about fifteen hundred paces' outside the city and corrects an earlier figure of 2.5 km.
stops.campa: The hillside does not stay empty. By the fourth century a church stands over the cave, and around it cells for men and cells for women, and a wall enclosing the whole. Pilgrims come up the road from Seleucia, women in particular, and the book about her is read aloud in the church built on the place the book describes. The site is called Hagia Thekla, and later Meryemlik. Fifteen hundred paces, by the pilgrims' own measure, from the city gate up to the cave.
suggested_refs: Egeria, Itinerarium 22-23, c. 384: the cells, the wall, the deaconess Marthana, and the reading aloud of Thecla's acts at the shrine
Gregory of Nazianzus, who withdrew to this sanctuary and listed Thecla among the martyrs he venerated
sources: Wikipedia, 'Aya Tekla Church' (fetched): 'A pilgrimage site dedicated to her existed by 374'; 'By 384, pilgrim Egeria documented numerous monastic cells for men and women, and a central church with an enclosing wall'
Wikipedia, 'Egeria (pilgrim)' (fetched)
Wikipedia, 'Thecla' (fetched)

stops.name: Hagia Thekla, the forty-six miracles
stops.date_confidence: the text is attested and its Seleucian setting is confirmed by Wikipedia's Thecla article; the dating c. 445-474 comes from the dossier and was not independently verified against a primary or academic source in this pass. The attribution to Basil of Seleucia is now rejected; the author is anonymous.
stops.campa: In the fifth century somebody at the sanctuary writes down what she has been doing there. Forty-six miracles: cures, dreams, rescues, and a fair number of arguments, because she appears to the clergy of her own shrine to correct them and appears to pilgrims to tell them what the clergy will not. She is not remote in these stories. She turns up in a room, says something short, and is gone. The man she said it to writes it down and carries it to the priest, who has usually already heard from her himself.
suggested_refs: The anonymous Life and Miracles of Saint Thecla, mid to late 5th century, formerly ascribed to Basil of Seleucia
sources: Wikipedia, 'Thecla' (fetched): 'A 5th-century anonymous work, The Life and Miracles of Thecla, focused on this location'

stops.name: Hagia Thekla, the basilica on the crest
stops.date_confidence: attested that Zeno commissioned the hilltop basilica; the dating is contradictory and is left so. Wikipedia's Aya Tekla article dates the building 460-470, which precedes Zeno's accession in January 474; the Thecla article says only 5th century. The Wikipedia biography of Zeno mentions neither Thecla nor the shrine. The 55 by 37 m measurement comes from a source that returned 404 at every URL form tried this pass.
stops.campa: An emperor pays for the next building. Zeno, who credits her with the return of his throne, raises a basilica on the crest above the cave, some fifty-five metres by thirty-seven, with cisterns, a bath, and an aqueduct bringing water along the ridge. The dates the sources give for the building do not agree with the dates they give for his reign. For two centuries this is one of the great pilgrimage complexes of the eastern Mediterranean. The cave church stays underneath it all, cut into the rock and reached by steps.
suggested_refs: Ernst Herzfeld and Samuel Guyer's 1907 survey of Meriamlik, published as Meriamlik und Korykos, MAMA II (1930)
sources: Wikipedia, 'Aya Tekla Church' (fetched): 'Emperor Zeno commissioned the prominent hilltop basilica between 460-470 CE'
Wikipedia, 'Thecla' (fetched): 'restored by Emperor Zeno in the 5th century'
Wikipedia, 'Zeno (emperor)' (fetched), for the reign of January 474 to April 491

stops.name: Rome, the catacomb on the Via Ostiense
stops.date_confidence: attested as a fourth-century catacomb bearing her name, cut into a reused first-century pagan necropolis; rediscovered in 1870 by Mariano Armellini, with the frescoes laser-cleaned by Barbara Mazzei's team in 2008-2010 and announced by the Vatican in June 2010. Coordinates are derived from the description of the southern Ostiense quarter and are not surveyed. No claim is made that Thecla is buried here.
stops.campa: Under the southern Ostiense quarter of Rome, near where the Laurentina road leaves, a fourth-century catacomb is cut into an older pagan burying ground and carries her name. Nobody claims she is in it. The Roman church gave a cemetery to a woman from Lycaonia who never came there, and Roman families were buried in her keeping for a century. Forgotten afterwards and lost under the fields, it was found again in 1870. In one chamber, cleaned by laser in 2010, is a painted head thought to be the oldest surviving image of Paul.
suggested_refs: The late-fourth-century portrait of Paul in the Catacomb of Saint Thecla, with Peter, John and Andrew
sources: Wikipedia, 'Catacomb of Saint Thecla' (fetched)
Wikipedia, 'Thecla' (fetched), on the June 2010 Vatican announcement

stops.name: Ephesus, the woman in the grotto of Paul
stops.date_confidence: disputed at every level, and unconfirmed in this pass. The fresco's date, the identification of the woman as Thecla, and the motive for the damage cannot all be established. No academic source could be reached: dedicated articles returned 404 and Wikipedia's main Ephesus article does not mention it. The pin is the general Ephesus site, not the grotto.
stops.campa: In a rock chamber above Ephesus, on a wall painted at the end of the fourth century, Paul sits with a scroll, and beside him a woman stands with her hand raised in the gesture a teacher uses, and the name written beside her is read by most as Thecla. Somebody scratched out her eyes and destroyed her raised hand, and left the man next to her untouched. Whether that was done to an image or to a woman shown teaching cannot now be settled from the plaster.
suggested_refs: The so-called Grotto of Paul above Ephesus and its damaged double portrait
sources: Reported in the research dossier for this subject; no independent academic or encyclopedic source reachable in this pass

stops.name: The Mareotis, the flasks of Menas and Thecla
stops.date_confidence: the Egyptian material corpus is a synthesis carried from the dossier and was not re-fetched from a specific academic source in this pass. Coordinates are a regional placement in the Mareotis lakeland southwest of Alexandria, not an excavated site; the ampullae themselves are the mass-produced pilgrim flasks of Abu Mena, which lies further southwest.
stops.campa: In the lakeland southwest of Alexandria she becomes an Egyptian saint. Coptic women take her for their patron in virginity and in sickness, and her face goes onto wall paintings and funerary stelae, onto lamps and combs and woven cloth. At the great shrine of Menas the potters turn out clay flasks by the thousand for pilgrims to carry holy oil home in, and on one side of the flask is Menas between his camels, and on the other side is Thecla standing between two beasts with her arms out.
suggested_refs: Abu Mena pilgrim ampullae pairing Menas and Thecla, the commonest surviving objects of her cult
sources: Dossier synthesis of Coptic material evidence, not independently re-verified
Wikipedia, 'Thecla' (fetched), for the Menas association

stops.name: Rome, the grave beside Paul
stops.date_confidence: a late variant tradition with no date of its own; the date here is an ordering device only. It is incompatible with the Seleucian ending and with Maaloula. The Wikipedia article on the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls contains no mention of Thecla, so the claim rests on the variant endings alone.
stops.campa: One family of manuscripts refuses the cave and the mountain altogether. In them Thecla does not stay in Isauria. She goes on to Rome to look for Paul, arrives to find him already dead, and lies down near his grave and is buried there beside the road out of the city, in the ground that later carries his basilica. Nothing at the basilica remembers this. The tradition exists only inside the endings of her own book, and it cannot be true at the same time as the rock at Seleucia.
suggested_refs: The Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls, on the Via Ostiense
sources: Variant endings of the Acts of Paul and Thecla, per NASSCAL e-Clavis (fetched) on the eight distinct Greek conclusions
Wikipedia, 'Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls' (fetched), which does not mention Thecla

stops.name: Maaloula, the mountain that opened
stops.date_confidence: local tradition with no date of its own; the date is an ordering device. This version has the rock open to let her out, where the Seleucian version has the rock close on her, and the two cannot both stand. Coordinates are for the town, since the fetched article gives none for the convent itself.
stops.campa: In the Qalamoun mountains north of Damascus a village sits at the mouth of a gorge, and the gorge is the story. Thecla, pursued, comes to the ridge and can go no further; she prays; the mountain splits from top to bottom and she walks out through the crack. The village takes its Aramaic name from that opening, roughly the entrance, and the people there still speak the language the name is in. Seleucia says the rock closed on her. Maaloula says the rock opened and let her through.
suggested_refs: The gorge at Maaloula and the Western Neo-Aramaic still spoken in the village
sources: Wikipedia, 'Maaloula' (fetched)

stops.name: Mosfiloti, the spring under Helena's monastery
stops.date_confidence: the monastery and its spring are attested at Mosfiloti, inland from Larnaca, per Wikipedia; the foundation by Helena is tradition, and the arrival of relics with refugees from the Mamluk conquest of Cilicia is dated only loosely to the 14th or 15th century. Coordinates corrected in this pass: earlier figures pointed at the unrelated Agia Thekla beach near Ayia Napa.
stops.campa: On Cyprus, inland from Larnaca at Mosfiloti, a monastery of nuns keeps her name and a spring whose water is taken for diseases of the skin. The foundation is credited to Helena, mother of Constantine, on her way back from Jerusalem. What is documented is later: when the Mamluks took Cilicia, Christians crossed the water carrying whatever they could lift, and relics said to be Thecla's came over with them and were put here. The date of that crossing is given only as the fourteenth century or the fifteenth.
suggested_refs: The Agia Thekla monastery at Mosfiloti and its healing spring
sources: Wikipedia, 'Thecla' (fetched): 'the monastery of Saint Tecla that is located in Mosfiloti near Larnaca'
Wikipedia, 'Mosfiloti' (fetched), for coordinates and the spring

stops.name: Maaloula, twelve nuns taken from Mar Takla
stops.date_confidence: attested, with a two-day discrepancy left standing: Wikipedia's Thecla article dates the seizure to Monday 2 December 2013, its Maaloula article dates the capture of the town to 3 December 2013. Both give twelve nuns; an earlier figure of thirteen nuns and three attendants is unsupported by either. Release 9 March 2014, negotiated through Lebanese officials.
stops.campa: The cave and the spring above the gorge became a convent, Mar Takla, and it is still one. Water runs out of the rock beside her cave and pilgrims come for it, Christian and Muslim both, and drink it and carry it away in bottles. In December 2013 fighters of the Nusra Front took the town and took twelve of the nuns; they were released the following March, exchanged for about a hundred and fifty Syrian women held by the government, and went back to the convent.
suggested_refs: The Greek Orthodox convent of Mar Takla at Maaloula, its cave and its spring
sources: Wikipedia, 'Maaloula' (fetched)
Wikipedia, 'Thecla' (fetched)

segments.name: Tarragona, and the Arm out of Armenia

stops.name: Tarragona, the arm out of Armenia
stops.date_confidence: the translation is dated 1319-1323 by the study NASSCAL cites, La traslacion del brazo de Santa Tecla desde Armenia a Tarragona (1319-1323); other accounts give a bare 1321, which is the date used here to fix the stop in sequence. The relic's biological identity has never been tested.
stops.campa: The Armenian kingdom in Cilicia is falling and its treasuries are being emptied westward. Between 1319 and 1323 an arm said to be Thecla's is negotiated out of Armenia and carried to Tarragona in Catalonia, where the archbishopric has lately been restored and needs a patron with a history behind her. The city takes her. From the fourteenth century the cathedral chapter carries her name, and so does the September feast, and the arm is carried at the head of the procession.
suggested_refs: La traslacion del brazo de Santa Tecla desde Armenia a Tarragona (1319-1323), cited by NASSCAL
sources: NASSCAL, 'Altarpiece and Chapel of Thecla, Tarragona Cathedral' (fetched)
Wikipedia, 'Tarragona Cathedral' (fetched), for coordinates

stops.name: Tarragona, the alabaster and the hand out of the rock
stops.date_confidence: attested. The white marble altar is dated about 1220 to Archbishop Asparec; the alabaster retable is dated 1426-1434 to Johan Vallfogona. The panel showing the arm emerging from the rock derives from a text called the Virtuous Deeds of Thecla and is a legend generated to explain the relic; no manuscript of the Acts contains it.
stops.campa: Tarragona builds her a life in stone. Around 1220 the archbishop commissions a white marble altar carved with her story around a central figure blessing her; between 1426 and 1434 Johan Vallfogona cuts an alabaster retable, Mary and Christ above, Thecla and Paul standing at either side, six scenes from her book in relief below. One of the panels shows something no manuscript of the Acts contains: the rock she vanished into, and an arm coming back out of it, into the hands of waiting clergy.
suggested_refs: The Vallfogona alabaster retable in Tarragona Cathedral, and the Virtuous Deeds of Thecla behind its relic panel
sources: NASSCAL, 'Altarpiece and Chapel of Thecla, Tarragona Cathedral' (fetched)

stops.name: Tarragona, the chapel and the human towers
stops.date_confidence: contradiction left standing. NASSCAL dates the chapel to Josep Prat i Delorta, 1760-1775; Wikipedia's Tarragona Cathedral article dates its construction to 1777, in late Baroque, over the former baptistery. The stop is dated 1777 and both figures are recorded.
stops.campa: The chapter puts up a late Baroque chapel over the old baptistery to hold the arm, finished in the 1770s, and the arm has been carried out of it every September since. Tarragona keeps her as its patron, and the September festival fills the streets below the cathedral with processions, giants, devils, and the castells, the human towers that go up storey by storey until a child climbs to the top of one and raises a hand. The child at the top is called the enxaneta.
suggested_refs: The Chapel of Santa Tecla, Tarragona Cathedral, and the Festes de Santa Tecla each September
sources: Wikipedia, 'Tarragona Cathedral' (fetched): 'Chapel of St. Tecla, patroness of Tarragona, built in 1777 in late Baroque style'
NASSCAL, 'Altarpiece and Chapel of Thecla, Tarragona Cathedral' (fetched)
